{"filepath":"ev_connector_research.md","content":"# EV Connector Standards: concise technical & procurement briefing (2026-09)

Prepared: 2026-09-06

This document summarizes competing EV charging connector standards (minimum: CCS1/CCS2, CHAdeMO including ChaoJi, NACS/Tesla, GB/T, IEC Type 2/Type 1). For each standard I list: typical AC and DC power ranges, max charging speeds (deployed & spec), regional adoption and regulatory status, vehicle compatibility, common use-cases, installation/equipment cost drivers, interoperability/adapters, major manufacturers/operators, and recent market/standardization trends or transition risks. Sources are listed at the end.

---

## Quick legend
- AC = alternating current (usually Level 1/2/Mode 2 or Mode 3 charging; uses vehicle on-board charger)
- DC = direct current fast charging (bypasses on-board charger; charger supplies battery voltage/current)
- kW = kilowatt; A = ampere; V = volt

---

## Combined Charging System (CCS1 / CCS2)
Summary: CCS is the dominant international DC fast‑charging architecture outside China/Japan historic pockets; CCS1 is the North American physical variant (Combo 1 / J1772 top), CCS2 (Combo 2 / Type 2 top) is used widely in Europe and many export markets.

- Typical AC power (when using the integrated Type 1/Type 2 AC contacts):
  - CCS1 (J1772 top): single‑phase AC commonly 3.7–19.2 kW (typical home/workplace chargers 7.2–19.2 kW depending on OBC and breaker).
  - CCS2 (Type 2 top): single‑phase or three‑phase AC, typical 3.7–22 kW; three‑phase installations and OBCs can support up to ~43 kW in some vehicles.

- Typical DC power / max charging speeds:
  - Common public DC fast chargers: 50–350 kW (most public deployments 50–350 kW in 2020s).
  - Deployed ultra‑fast CCS: 350 kW widely, 350–500 kW sites exist (liquid‑cooled cables); CCS specifications support ~1000 V and 500 A (practical upper limits ~500 kW today in production deployments).

- Regional adoption & regulatory status:
  - CCS2 is the mandated/market‑dominant DC fast standard across the EU and much of Europe; CCS1 historically used in North America but market share there has been challenged by NACS (see NACS section).
  - Many national/regional charging‑network rollouts in Europe (public fast networks, motorway chargers) are CCS2 first.

- Vehicle compatibility:
  - Broad OEM support in Europe: nearly all non‑Tesla EVs sold in Europe use CCS2 for DC fast charging. North American EVs historically used CCS1 or J1772+CCS; many OEMs committed to NACS in NA (see NACS), but many fleet and older EVs remain CCS‑equipped.

- Common use‑cases:
  - Public motorway / corridor fast charging (50–350 kW stalls), destination fast charging.
  - Depot/fleet DC fast chargers for quick turnarounds (50–350 kW), especially for medium/heavy vehicles where CCS is adopted.
  - On‑board charger (AC) limits determine AC charging speed; for many EVs OBC is 7–22 kW.

- Installation & equipment cost drivers:
  - Site electrical service capacity (transformer, service upgrades) and grid connection costs.
  - Cable type (air‑cooled vs liquid‑cooled for >350 kW), pedestal/hardware, civil works, network communications and software (OCPP), permitting and trenching.
  - Higher power requires larger breakers, upgraded conductors, and often three‑phase service — major cost increases above ~150 kW per stall.

- Interoperability / adapter availability:
  - CCS is an open, widely supported standard; many chargers are multi‑standard or offer CCS plus other connectors.
  - Adaptation to/from other standards is limited: CCS↔CHAdeMO adapters historically exist only in niche/legacy forms; NACS↔CCS adapters are available from third parties and some OEMs/networks (see NACS notes).

- Major manufacturers / operators supporting it:
  - Charger OEMs: ABB, Siemens, Tritium, Delta, EVBox, Alpitronic, ZEV, Ingeteam; many vendors produce CCS DC chargers.
  - Network operators: Ionity (Europe), Electrify America (US), IONITY partners, many utility and independent operators use CCS2.

- Recent market/standardization trends & transition risks:
  - Trend: CCS remains the default EU standard; CCS implementations push higher power (liquid‑cooled cables, 350–500 kW). The installed base is large and interoperable in Europe.
  - Risk: In North America, part of the market has shifted to NACS, reducing long‑term growth of CCS1 plugs in some NA deployments; fleets that operate in cross‑border or global contexts should account for mixed infrastructure.

Sources (CCS):
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combined_Charging_System
- https://www.fiverevse.com/news/What-is-a-CCS2-Charger-Fast-and-Ultra-Fast-EV-Charging-Solution.html
- https://plughopper.com/ev-charging/ccs1
- https://zencar.net/ccs1-vs-ccs2
- https://www.mxpcharger.com/what-is-the-difference-between-ccs1-and-ccs2

---

## CHAdeMO (including ChaoJi / CHAdeMO 3.x)
Summary: CHAdeMO is (historically) Japan’s DC fast‑charging connector family and protocol. The association and China’s standards organizations have collaborated on the next‑generation ‘ChaoJi’ (also discussed as CHAdeMO 3.x / ChaoJi) to create a high‑power interoperable plug, but legacy CHAdeMO still exists in many Japanese and some global deployments.

- Typical AC power:
  - CHAdeMO is a DC fast standard; local AC charging on vehicles in Japan typically uses Type 1 (J1772) or vehicle‑specific inlets—on‑board charger limits vary (3.7–22 kW typical).

- Typical DC power / max charging speeds:
  - Legacy CHAdeMO (early generations): 50–62.5 kW (commonly 50 kW stalls on early networks).
  - CHAdeMO 2.0 / newer published specs: support for 400 kW class in upgraded protocols.
  - ChaoJi / CHAdeMO 3.x (co‑developed with China/CEC): designed for ultra‑high power — published numbers include designs targeting 500 kW and up to 900 kW/1+ MW class capability (spec language varies by source); practical deployments in 2020s remain lower while testing and standardization continue.

- Regional adoption & regulatory status:
  - Strong legacy adoption in Japan (many chargers and early Japanese EVs used CHAdeMO). Outside Japan, CHAdeMO was used in some early deployments (Nissan Leaf) but CCS largely displaced CHAdeMO in Europe.
  - ChaoJi is an industry effort (CHAdeMO + China Electricity Council collaboration) to harmonize and produce a next‑generation plug — adoption depends on IEC/regulatory recognition and OEM/network uptake.

- Vehicle compatibility:
  - Historically: Nissan Leaf, Mitsubishi and other Japanese EVs used CHAdeMO.
  - Newer Japanese and Chinese OEMs are participating in ChaoJi work; long‑term compatibility will depend on OEM hardware choices.

- Common use‑cases:
  - Public fast charging in Japan and some export markets; depot/fleet use in regions where Japanese EVs dominate.
  - Legacy stations for passenger cars; ChaoJi is targeted at high‑power public and commercial charging (buses, trucks).

- Installation & equipment cost drivers:
  - Same grid/service and cable costs as CCS; ChaoJi / high‑power implementations will require liquid‑cooled cables and significant distribution upgrades for >350 kW deployments.

- Interoperability / adapters:
  - CHAdeMO legacy adapters exist for some vehicle/charger pairs; ChaoJi aims to harmonize with GB/T efforts to ease cross‑compatibility between China and Japan.
  - Adapters between CHAdeMO and CCS are uncommon and limited; conversion requires protocol and hardware translation.

- Major manufacturers / operators supporting it:
  - CHAdeMO Association (standard body); major Japanese OEMs historically (Nissan, Mitsubishi). ChaoJi joint activity involves CHAdeMO and China Electricity Council.

- Recent market/standardization trends & transition risks:
  - Trend: CHAdeMO’s market share outside Japan declined in favor of CCS; ChaoJi is a strategic attempt to re‑establish a high‑power unified interface and align with GB/T.
  - Risk: If ChaoJi does not achieve broad IEC/market endorsement or if OEMs prefer CCS/NACS, investment in CHAdeMO/ChaoJi‑only infrastructure could become stranded or niche.

Sources (CHAdeMO / ChaoJi):
- https://www.chademo.com/technology/high-power
- https://www.chademo.com/chaoji-gbt-standards-released
- https://www.worldstandards.eu/cars/connector-types/chaoji
- https://nvdungx.github.io/CHAdeMO-specification-and-software-design
- https://www.patsnap.com/resources/blog/articles/ev-fast-charging-interface-technology-landscape-2026-2
- https://www.elinkpower.com/news/the-chademo-standard-for-charging-in-japan-a-comprehensive-overview

## NACS (North American Charging Standard; Tesla connector)
Summary: NACS (SAE J3400) is the Tesla‑originated compact connector that combines AC and DC contacts in a single slim plug. Since 2022–2025 several major OEMs and charging networks publicly committed to adopt NACS in North America; this has driven rapid roll‑out of NACS ports on third‑party sites and widespread interest.

- Typical AC power:
  - AC via NACS (vehicle and charger dependent) typically supports Level 2 AC charging at 7–11.5 kW (residential/AC wallbox / Tesla Wall Connector class values) up to higher three‑phase rates where implemented outside NA.

- Typical DC power / max charging speeds:
  - Tesla Superchargers in service commonly provide 120–250 kW per vehicle (V2, V3), with some newer stalls offering higher rates; the NACS specification as maintained by SAE/J3400 documents electrical limits that enable much higher power (vendor claims/specs indicate capability for several hundred kW and theoretical headroom to ~1,000 V / high currents).
  - Deployed public non‑Tesla NACS chargers (Electrify America, ChargePoint, independent stations) largely mirror CCS-class power ranges (50–350 kW) while Tesla Superchargers are frequently 150–250 kW per vehicle in real world.

- Regional adoption & regulatory status:
  - Rapid adoption in North America since OEMs and major networks announced migration plans (2023–2025 era); Tesla opened the Supercharger design/protocol under SAE stewardship (NACS/SAE J3400) to encourage take‑up.
  - NACS is not yet mandated in most jurisdictions but has strong industry momentum in NA.

- Vehicle compatibility:
  - Tesla vehicles (native) use NACS. Since 2023 multiple OEMs announced planned NACS ports on new vehicles or adapter strategies for North America — increasing native compatibility across brands.

- Common use‑cases:
  - Tesla Supercharger network for long‑distance travel (reliable, networked fast charging).
  - Third‑party adoption of NACS connector allows non‑Tesla OEM EVs to access Supercharger network and gives fleets access to high‑uptime Tesla sites when agreements are in place.

- Installation & equipment cost drivers:
  - Similar grid/service, cooling and civil work drivers as CCS; for high‑power systems wiring, power distribution and cable cooling are the main incremental costs.
  - Operators retrofitting existing CCS sites to add NACS docks face costs for new pedestals, adapter hardware or multi‑standard charging assemblies (e.g., Tesla Magic Dock designs).

- Interoperability / adapters:
  - NACS↔CCS adapters (vehicle‑side or charger‑side) are commercially available from third parties and some OEMs and charge‑point operators provide dual‑connector pedestals to preserve coverage across legacy vehicles.
  - Tesla has produced/endorsed physical adapters and the network access policies (billing/auth) are being updated to allow non‑Tesla OEM access in many markets.

- Major manufacturers / operators supporting it:
  - Tesla (originator & largest network operator). Third‑party networks and OEMs (announced transitions by several major automakers and charging network operators) have been adding NACS connectors across North America.

- Recent market/standardization trends & transition risks:
  - Trend: Rapid industry movement in North America toward NACS has led many networks to add NACS plugs or multi‑output chargers. This materially changes the connector landscape in NA.
  - Risk: Transition costs and dual‑support complexity while fleets still operate CCS‑only vehicles; global fleets operating in both NA and Europe/Asia will face mixed requirements.

Sources (NACS/Tesla):
- https://www.tesla.com/blog/opening-north-american-charging-system
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Charging_Standard
- https://www.jdpower.com/cars/shopping-guides/what-is-the-north-american-charging-standard-nacs
- https://simpleswitch.io/nacs-charging-standard
- https://ev-lectron.com/blogs/blog/what-is-nacs-a-complete-guide-to-the-new-charging-standard

## GB/T (China national standard)
Summary: GB/T is China’s national EV charging standard family (separate AC and DC connectors/protocols). It is mandatory for vehicles sold in mainland China and dominates China’s charging network. China’s GB/T work and the ChaoJi collaboration aim at high‑power harmonization.

- Typical AC power:
  - GB/T AC (domestic chargers) generally supports single‑phase and three‑phase AC for typical onboard chargers; typical AC L2 values are comparable to Type 2 (e.g., 3.7–22 kW commonly), subject to vehicle OBC limits.

- Typical DC power / max charging speeds:
  - Deployed DC chargers in China commonly range from 50 kW to 240 kW+ for passenger EVs; updated GB/T and related documents and ChaoJi collaboration specify high‑power capability (published figures include support up to 1.2 MW / 1,500 V × high current in the latest high‑power documents), intended to cover buses/trucks and ultra‑fast passenger charging.

- Regional adoption & regulatory status:
  - GB/T is the national standard in mainland China and is effectively required for domestic vehicles and most Chinese chargers. Foreign OEMs selling in China provide GB/T inlets for local sales.

- Vehicle compatibility:
  - All new EVs sold in mainland China are required to use GB/T connectors for local charging (or provide supported adapters); many Chinese OEMs and commercial vehicles adopt GB/T for DC charging.

- Common use‑cases:
  - China’s rapidly expanded public DC fast network (corridor and city chargers), depot chargers for buses and trucks, and dedicated fast chargers for passenger cars.

- Installation & equipment cost drivers:
  - Same high‑power drivers: transformer/service upgrades, liquid‑cooled cables for very high power, permitting and site civil works. High‑power GB/T/ChaoJi installations aimed at buses/trucks will require major distribution upgrades and potentially dedicated substations.

- Interoperability / adapters:
  - GB/T uses different plug shapes and protocol; outside China, adapters and converter boxes are required to charge GB/T‑equipped vehicles.
  - ChaoJi collaboration aims to harmonize some mechanical/electrical aspects with CHAdeMO to reduce fragmentation.

- Major manufacturers / operators supporting it:
  - Domestic charger OEMs and state/market operators in China (State Grid, local charger manufacturers, large OEMs) broadly support GB/T.

- Recent market/standardization trends & transition risks:
  - Trend: China is moving to higher power GB/T revisions and aligning some work with ChaoJi; the scale of China’s installed base makes GB/T deeply entrenched for the Chinese market.
  - Risk: Global fleets that export/import vehicles between China and other markets will need adapters or multiple inlet strategies; investments in GB/T‑only infrastructure are primarily China‑specific.

Sources (GB/T):
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GB/T_charging_standard
- https://www.vector.com/us/en/know-how/protocols/gbt-27930
- https://www.chademo.com/chaoji-gbt-standards-released
- https://www.greencarreports.com/news/1140871_china-updates-its-ev-charging-standard-claims-cross-compatibility

---

## IEC Type 2 (Mennekes) and Type 1 (SAE J1772) — AC inlet standards
Summary: Type 1 (SAE J1772) and Type 2 (IEC 62196) are the AC charging connector standards that form the basis of many combined DC connectors (CCS extensions) and are the typical Level‑2 charging interfaces used for home/workplace/destination charging.

- Typical AC power:
  - Type 1 (SAE J1772): single‑phase AC, common values 3.7–7.4 kW for many older installations; some implementations support up to 19.2 kW (80 A @ 240 V) depending on vehicle OBC and site.
  - Type 2 (IEC 62196‑2 / Mennekes): single‑phase or three‑phase AC. Typical values 3.7–22 kW (single‑ or three‑phase); full spec supports up to ~43 kW (3×63 A @ 230/400 V nominal in some configurations).

- Max charging speeds (realistic/on‑board limits):
  - Most passenger EVs’ on‑board chargers (OBC) are in the 3.7–22 kW range; some premium or commercial vehicles have OBCs supporting 22–43 kW.

- Regional adoption & regulatory status:
  - Type 2 is the mandated/standardised AC inlet across Europe for public AC charging (Mode 3). Type 1 was common in North America and Japan for AC Level 2 but is increasingly replaced by combined CCS connectors on newer models in some markets.

- Vehicle compatibility:
  - European EVs almost always use Type 2 inlets for AC; many North American and Japanese legacy/historical vehicles use Type 1 for AC.

- Common use‑cases:
  - Home charging, workplace charging, overnight depot charging for fleet vehicles (AC charging is lower cost and used when vehicles can dwell overnight/multi‑hour).
  - OBC size defines charging time — depot planning must consider per‑vehicle OBC kW and dwell time.

- Installation & equipment cost drivers:
  - Level‑2 AC installations generally require a dedicated breaker and a professionally installed EVSE; costs scale with number of circuits, meter/management hardware, load management (to avoid panel upgrades), and smart network connectivity.

- Interoperability / adapters:
  - AC adapters are common (travel adapters between household sockets and J1772/Type 2 hardware, Type 1↔Type 2 passive adapters exist but are limited by vehicle inlet and wiring policy).
  - For fleets, standardized AC sockets (Type 2 in Europe) reduce adapter complexity.

- Major manufacturers / operators supporting it:
  - Virtually all EV manufacturers supply vehicles with Type 2 (EU) or Type 1/J1772 (legacy NA/Japan) AC inlets; EVSE manufacturers worldwide support these connectors for Level‑2 charging.

- Recent market/standardization trends & transition risks:
  - Trend: Europe remains firmly Type 2 for AC; many markets are converging on combined‑connector strategies (e.g., CCS2 uses Type 2 top) so AC standardization is stable in most regions.
  - Risk: For global fleets, mixed Type 1/Type 2 history requires planning for adapters or dual‑fitted chargers in depots.

Sources (Type 1 / Type 2):
- https://driivz.com/blog/ev-charging-standards-and-protocols
- https://www.power-sonic.com/guide-to-level-2-ev-charging
- https://injetenergy.com/blog/the-complete-guide-to-ev-charging-connectors-types-standards-compatibility-2026
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combined_Charging_System

---

## Consolidated observations and transition risks (cross‑standard)
- High‑power convergence: industry work (ChaoJi / GB/T harmonization, and manufacturer/network moves) is pushing standards toward higher power capability (350 kW and above, with liquid‑cooled cables and higher voltage architectures). This reduces connector divergence at the technical capability level but raises interoperability and market risks during migration.
- Regional entrenchment: Europe = CCS2 + Type 2 for AC; China = GB/T (with ChaoJi work ongoing); Japan = historic CHAdeMO base with ChaoJi harmonization efforts; North America (2023–2026) saw rapid NACS adoption momentum. Fleets that operate across regions will need multi‑standard strategies.
- Adapter & retrofit realities: adapters exist (notably NACS↔CCS), and many networks deploy multi‑connector pedestals. However, adapters are a compromise (power/communication limits, warranty/insurance implications) and are not a universal solution for high‑power operations (liquid‑cooled cables and safety interlocks complicate adaptation).
- Fleet electrification nuance: on‑vehicle on‑board charger size controls AC charging capability and has little impact on DC charging speed (which is determined by battery chemistry, thermal management and max DC charge acceptance). Investing in high‑power DC capacity is necessary only when duty cycles require short turnarounds.

## 3 concise, actionable implications for a fleet buyer
1. Prioritise uptime with multi‑standard access: specify chargers and stalls that accept the connector family used by your current fleet and include at least one alternative connector type (or an approved adapter strategy) per site to avoid vehicle incompatibility during mixed‑fleet operations or OEM transitions (e.g., CCS + NACS options in North America; CCS2 + Type 2 in Europe; GB/T in China).

2. Future‑proof for power and protocol: size electrical service and civil work for your expected peak per‑stall power (plan for 150–350 kW if you need fast/turnaround charging, and allow substation/transformer upgrades and liquid‑cooled cable routing). Avoid building only low‑power DC unless duty cycles and OBC limits justify it — overprovision capacity now is cheaper than repeated civil rework later.

3. Procurement & installation checklist items:
   - Require OCPP (or equivalent) and open network interoperability, metering and clear billing APIs in chargers. 
   - Contractually require capability to add/replace connectors (adapter or swap‑out pedestals) and specify cooling and cable mounting standards for future >350 kW retrofits.
   - Include warranty/insurance review for adapter use and ensure supplier experience with multi‑protocol installations; plan for grid upgrade timelines and permitting in your project schedule.

Prepared by: Research Specialist (AI‑assisted summary)

Where multiple specification revisions or collaborative initiatives (e.g., ChaoJi) exist, I report commonly published capability ranges and highlight where practical deployments lag the highest theoretical values. For procurement decisions, confirm vendor electrical specs, local regulatory mandates, and OEM vehicle inlet choices at contract stage.
